extracted.intended_audience: public relations counselors, advertisers, political campaigners, and business leaders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and executing mass-publicity and propaganda campaigns for commercial products or political causes, covering audience analysis, budgeting, media selection, staging events, and crisis handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address inter-commodity and inter-industrial competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter-commodity competition (between products used alternatively for the same purpose) and inter-industrial competition (between apparently unrelated industries which affect each other or compete for the consumer's dollar) are new forms of competition which 'cannot be fought single-handed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coordinated action by trade associations and joint efforts when products compete across commodities (examples: oranges vs. pineapples, linoleum vs. carpets). Recognize food industries as especially subject to this new competition due to consumption limits; call upon associations to help rather than acting alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use large-scale mass events and media hook-ups to concentrate attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass broadcasts and national hook-ups can concentrate unprecedented attention on a product (e.g., the Dodge Victory Six nation-wide hook-up reaching an estimated thirty million Americans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan spectacular launches or broadcasts to produce a 'sugar-coated sales message' that reaches a very large, concentrated audience; be prepared for the expense (example: $60,000 broadcast cost, $25,000 aggregate artists' fee). Balance reach against cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and justify added cost for attractive modes of appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: All modes of sales appeal require spending money to make the appeal attractive; celebrity endorsements or pictures add cost though not to the product itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh cost versus persuasive effect—modern tendency may be to reduce cost (e.g., eliminate premiums), but recognize that investments (pictures, distinguished endorsements, celebrities) may be necessary to secure public attention and appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate beyond price using style and minor product modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: If low price is the only basis of competition, cut-throat price wars remove profit and incentive; the solution is to develop some sales appeal other than mere cheapness and give the product 'some element of originality' to distinguish it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use principles familiar to propagandists—gregariousness, obedience to authority, emulation—to popularize minor elements as matters of style (examples: painting typewriters cheerful hues, reviving large hat fashions through coordinated shows). This allows mass production to coexist with profitable small specialty businesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use publicity and staged events to change consumer habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized events (fashion fetes, tableaux with artists, style committees, distinguished endorsements, mannequins parading to the trade) can alter buying habits and popularize a style nationwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring together society leaders, style experts, fashion editors, artists, and attractive models; create newsworthy events that the press and stores will distribute to consumers and buyers (example: millinery show leading to thousands of large hat sales).

rubrics_metrics.name: Call in public relations counsel to handle emergencies and false rumors promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: A false rumor may occasion enormous loss in prestige and money if not handled promptly and effectively (example: Hudson Motor Company's stock swing; Beech-Nut denial countered by a hometown testimonial event).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to damaging rumors with decisive, technically handled public-relations actions—personal testimonials, community demonstrations, authoritative denials, or events that convincingly rebut the false news; a mere denial may not carry as much conviction as well-orchestrated public testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuously study and 'have finger on the public pulse'
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern business must understand changes in the public mind and be prepared to interpret itself fairly and eloquently to changing opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct ongoing research into public tastes and knowledge; adapt products and communications as public taste improves. Use market analysis to inform product changes and presentation; calculate media reach and duplication when planning campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat political campaigns like business campaigns: set objectives and express them clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step in a political campaign is to determine objectives and express them exceedingly well in the current form—that is, as a platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out the entire campaign according to broad basic plans (platforms, planks, pledges, budgets, activities, personalities) as a business would its marketing plan. A clear statement of objectives should guide all propaganda activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure platforms and pledges are honest and credible
rubrics_metrics.description: In devising the platform the leader should be sure that it is an honest platform; campaign pledges and promises should not be lightly considered and 'ought to carry something of the guarantee principle and money-back policy' of honorable businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ephemeral or insincere pledges; public skepticism about campaign promotion arises because pledges are seen as 'written on the sand.' Honest, credible platforms increase public trust and campaign effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the public scientifically and segment audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: A survey of public desires and demands should be made as nearly scientific as possible to aid the political strategist or advertiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subdivide populations, avoid wasting effort on already-committed groups, and let analysis guide both product development and media selection. Use market/survey data to estimate repetition and overlap of national and local campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget and publicly manage fundraising and expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenses of the campaign should be budgeted like a business: decide how much money to raise, how to raise it, and how the money is to be spent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use business precedent to estimate campaign costs accurately; consider candid and public fundraising (charity-drive models) to raise prestige and public participation; allocate funds proportionately across media, events, personalities, and propaganda forms; small proportions may justify experiments, large proportions must be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate emotions with overall strategy and media
rubrics_metrics.description: To appeal to the emotions of the public is indispensable, but the emotional content must: (a) coincide in every way with the broad basic plans of the campaign and all its minor details; (b) be adapted to the many groups of the public at which it is to be aimed; and (c) conform to the media of the distribution of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid haphazard emotional stunts; use symbolic acts (e.g., kissing babies) only when synchronized with an actual plank or policy. Use parades, mass meetings, and other emotional formats when public interest is genuine; otherwise they are wasteful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize program effectiveness over mere personality
rubrics_metrics.description: Present-day politics places emphasis on personality, but the party and its aims are more important than the personality of the candidate; 'Not personality, but the ability of the candidate to carry out the party's program adequately, and the program itself should be emphasized.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personality strategically to sell a program, but ensure the candidate's ability and the program remain central in propaganda planning. The product (party program) should create the public image as well as the personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and target interlocking groups; educate emotions by group
rubrics_metrics.description: The public is made up of interlocking groups—economic, social, religious, educational, cultural, racial, collegiate, local, sports, and hundreds of others—so the campaign manager must educate the emotions in terms of groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify relevant groups and design appeals that align campaign issues with their personal interests (examples: inviting actors to court audiences who like amusements; the Shepard-Towner Maternity Bill's success due to mobilizing mothers, educators, physicians). Use group leaders to influence wider publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple media and varied events, synchronized
rubrics_metrics.description: The media through which a political campaign may be brought home are numerous: printed word (books, magazines, letters, posters), pictures (photographs, motion pictures), the ear (lectures, speeches, radio), and many more; events and activities must be created to put ideas into circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ radio, press, banquets, mass meetings, exhibitions, contests, educational cooperation, motion pictures, campaign songs, and other media in coordinated fashion. Do not put all one's eggs into one basket; synchronize all methods so they reinforce each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create circumstances and dramatize issues before direct argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than merely arguing an issue, a propagandist should create circumstances which set up trains of thought and dramatize the subject so the public will be keyed to the issue before direct appeals are made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage exhibitions, boycotts, expert endorsements, and demonstrations that make the contention self-evident (example: staging low-tariff exhibitions in multiple cities, dramatizing cost differences, organizing groups to boycott woolen clothes). When the public is primed, direct messages meet a receptive audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan timing for maximum media receptivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the entire world public and the press calendar when planning announcements (example: Masaryk changed the date of Czecho-Slovakia's proclamation to Monday so the press would give more coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule important events when media will have space and audiences will be receptive; small timing changes can produce greater international impact through cables and press reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain truthfulness and social utility to preserve propaganda effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The only propaganda that will tend to weaken itself as the world becomes more sophisticated is propaganda that is untrue or unsocial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure campaigns are not based on outright falsehoods or socially harmful claims; truthful and socially useful propaganda remains effective even as publics become more sophisticated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit news-dependence of media strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Because newspapers and reporters depend on politicians for news, the politician can often effectively control or influence coverage; the political leader must be a creator of circumstances, not a creature of mechanical processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlled release of information and create newsworthy circumstances so media dependence works to the campaign's advantage; do not rely solely on routine news processes—manufacture events that generate favorable coverage.
